# Secure property rights and land registry (`property_rights_land_registry`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: helped by surveying_triangulation, written_law_code, alphabet_writing
- Core idea: Every parcel of land is surveyed, mapped and entered in a public register with its owner and any mortgage; a sale or loan counts only once it is entered, and the state guarantees the entry. An owner who cannot be dispossessed by a stronger neighbour or the ruler will drain, plant and build; land with a clear title can be sold to whoever uses it best and pledged for credit; and the land tax can be assessed on measured area and quality instead of bargaining. Minimum design: parcel map, register of owners and charges, public access, and a court that follows the register.
- Pitfalls:
  - Registering only the claims of the powerful or the literate dispossesses everyone with customary, shared or seasonal rights (English enclosure, colonial titling)
  - A register that is not updated at every sale and inheritance is fiction within a generation (the Ming fish-scale registers were soon out of date)
  - Forgetting that people see a cadastre as a tax trap: they hide land, bribe surveyors or riot
  - Promising that titles alone create credit and growth: the evidence for de Soto's claim is mixed; courts, lenders and markets must exist too
  - Proposing private freehold where land belongs to lineage, village, temple or crown: it attacks the social order, not just a law
- History: mesopotamia: c. 2600 BC – sale documents for fields on clay and stone; c. 14th–12th c. BC Kassite kudurru boundary stones record royal land grants; egypt: pharaonic land surveys after each flood for tax; c. AD 70 Roman Egypt's bibliotheke enkteseon, a public archive of title and mortgages in each district; rome: surveyed land grids (centuriation) with bronze maps; AD 77 cadastre of Orange; china: 4th c. BC – Qin registers households and land; 1387 Ming fish-scale map registers (yulin tuce) of every plot; east_asia: 1582–1598 – Hideyoshi's cadastral survey (Taiko kenchi) measures Japan's fields by assessed yield; india: 1570s–1580s – Todar Mal's survey and assessment by measured area and crop under Akbar; islamic: 15th–16th c. – Ottoman tahrir survey registers of land, households and revenues; 1858 Ottoman Land Code and title registry; europe: 1086 – Domesday Book; c. 1130 Cologne's Schreinsbücher record urban property transfers; 1427 Florentine catasto; 1718–1760 Milanese mapped cadastre; 1807 Napoleonic cadastre; global: 1858 – Torrens system in South Australia: title by registration, guaranteed by the state
